content.text: Shuffled K-fold assumes every row is independent of the others. When several rows come from the same patient, or rows follow each other in time, a random split puts near-copies of the test rows in training and the score measures memory, not prediction. Split the way production will meet new data: by group, or by time.

A health-tech startup detects a condition from one-minute sensor recordings: 60 volunteers, 20 recordings each. A random forest scores 0.985 in shuffled 5-fold cross-validation, and the pilot with new patients is planned around that number. The pilot goes far worse. Re-evaluated with each volunteer's recordings kept in a single fold, the same model scores 0.686. It's better than chance, but most of the 0.985 was the model recognizing people it had already met.
The common misconception
Many developers treat shuffled K-fold as a valid evaluation for any dataset. It's an easy belief to hold:

items.text: It's the default in tutorials, and
shuffles unless you tell it not to.
Shuffling is often presented as good hygiene. scikit-learn's guide does say it can be essential when rows are sorted, for example by class.
Every row is tested exactly once, so the method feels thorough and fair.

content.text: The half-truth: K-fold is a sound estimator when rows are independent. It answers "how well will the model do on new rows like these?" With groups or time, the rows production sends aren't like a random slice of your table.
What actually happens

Cross-validation simulates deployment: train on what you'd have, test on what you'd meet. A random split simulates a world where tomorrow's rows are random draws from the same pool as yesterday's, the
i.i.d.

assumption. scikit-learn's guide notes that this assumption rarely holds in practice, and recommends time-aware splits for data generated over time and group-wise splits for data collected from different subjects, experiments or devices.
Groups: the model recognizes the person

Each patient's recordings share a personal signature: body shape, sensor placement, habits. Shuffle the rows and every validation fold holds recordings from patients whose other recordings are in training. A flexible model learns "this signature belongs to a sick patient" and looks brilliant. The script gives each patient a random signature and adds a real but weaker sign of the condition:

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, cross_val_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
patient = np.repeat(np.arange(60), 20)  # 60 patients, 20 recordings each
y = (rng.random(60) < 0.5)[patient]  # diagnosis, one per patient
X = rng.normal(size=(60, 10))[patient]  # each patient's own signature
X = X + 0.3 * rng.normal(size=(1200, 10))  # recording-to-recording noise
X[:, :2] += y[:, None]  # the real, weaker sign of the condition

model = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0)
cv = KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)  # rows dealt out at random
print(f"accuracy {cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=cv).mean():.3f}")
# accuracy 0.985

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, cross_val_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
patient = np.repeat(np.arange(60), 20)
y = (rng.random(60) < 0.5)[patient]
X = rng.normal(size=(60, 10))[patient]
X = X + 0.3 * rng.normal(size=(1200, 10))
X[:, :2] += y[:, None]

model = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0)
cv = GroupKFold(5)  # all of a patient's recordings in one fold
scores = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=cv, groups=patient)
print(f"accuracy {scores.mean():.3f}")
# accuracy 0.686

content.text: GroupKFold

guarantees that no patient appears in both the training and validation side of a fold, so the 0.686 answers the question the pilot asks: how well does it work on someone new? It also shows what the dataset really is: the diagnosis is decided once per patient, so you have 60 examples of sick or healthy people, not 1,200. Kapoor and Narayanan list this non-independence between training and test data as its own type of leakage, with a histopathology study that put different observations of the same patient on both sides.
Time: the model fills gaps instead of forecasting
Time series have
autocorrelation

: days next to each other look alike. Shuffle them and each test day sits between training days from just before and just after it, so the model interpolates. scikit-learn's guide warns that shuffling time-ordered data inflates the validation score for exactly this reason. The script forecasts a growing shop's daily sales from the last seven days, with a random forest and a linear model:

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, TimeSeriesSplit, cross_val_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
sales = 100 + np.cumsum(rng.normal(0.1, 2, 1010))  # a growing shop
X = np.column_stack([sales[i:i + 1000] for i in range(7)])  # last 7 days
y = sales[7:1007]  # the next day's sales
splits = {"shuffled": KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0),
          "forward": TimeSeriesSplit(5)}
models = {"forest": RandomForestRegressor(random_state=0),
          "linear": LinearRegression()}
for split_name, cv in splits.items():
    for model_name, model in models.items():
        mae = -cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=cv,
                               scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error").mean()
        print(f"{split_name:<8} {model_name}: MAE {mae:.2f}")
# shuffled forest: MAE 1.73
# shuffled linear: MAE 1.58
# forward  forest: MAE 5.48
# forward  linear: MAE 1.69

content.text: Shuffled, the two models look close: 1.73 against 1.58. Forward, the forest's error triples to 5.48 while the linear model barely moves, 1.69. A tree can only predict values in the range it saw in training, and a growing shop keeps reaching sales levels it has never had. Shuffling hid that, because every test day had training days at the same level around it.
TimeSeriesSplit
always trains on the past and tests on the next stretch, with training sets that grow fold by fold. Note that plain
cv=5

without shuffling doesn't fix this: it still trains on the future in every fold but the last. This isn't a toy problem either: Kapoor and Narayanan define temporal leakage as a test set holding data from before the training data, and found K-fold cross-validation on temporal data among the errors in the civil war prediction papers they tried to reproduce.

rows.text: Several rows per patient, user or device
Split by date, and keep test groups out of training

content.text: scikit-learn's "Visualizing cross-validation behavior" example plots which rows each splitter puts on each side. For your own data, print each fold's date range, and check that the patients or users in training and validation don't overlap. Two minutes of checking beats a pilot that misses by thirty points.
If a label covers a window, such as "churned within the next 30 days", or features average over the last week, the final training rows overlap the test period.
TimeSeriesSplit(gap=...)
drops that many samples between the end of each training set and its test set. Size it to the longest window.
How to apply it in your project
New patients, next month's orders, a new store? Write down the unit the model must generalize to.

items.title: Find the dependency in the data

content.text: Look for an identifier that repeats, such as a patient, user, device or session, and for a timestamp.
Pass
groups=
to
GroupKFold
or
StratifiedGroupKFold
, or sort by time and use
TimeSeriesSplit

items.title: Hold out the test set the same way

content.text: Keep unseen groups or the latest period for the final test. Google's Rules of ML: train on data up to a date, test on data after it.
A big drop from the shuffled score to the grouped or forward one measures how much the model was memorizing.
Key takeaways

items.text: Shuffled K-fold assumes independent rows; repeated subjects and time series break that assumption.
Grouped data: 0.985 with shuffled folds, 0.686 when each patient stayed in one fold.
Time series: shuffled folds hid that a forest's forecast error was 5.48, not 1.73.
